ownership_reason: Only the gold creates the encoder and the output buffer, sees the encoder's overflow result and can enlarge the buffer; hops 1-4 hand on the String and the Charset and get back one finished array, and none of them can change the gold's size estimate (the gold wraps the characters and takes the average bytes per char from an encoder it creates itself). Once the gold has returned the bytes that fit, the rest of the encoding is lost to every caller. The convention that the result holds the encoding of every character is pinned outside the gold: StringUtils.getBytesUtf16, the facade's sibling, returns the UTF-16 encoding with the byte-order mark and every character (String.getBytes(Charset)); Hex.encode(byte[]) encodes its hex String with the codec's charset the same way, and HexTest testRequiredCharset (UTF-16 included) and testCustomCharset (every available charset) assert that these bytes equal String.getBytes(name); BaseNCodec.ensureBufferSize enlarges the Base64/Base32 output buffer whenever the next output would not fit instead of dropping output; StringUtilsTest testGetBytesUtf16Be and testGetBytesUtf16Le assert that the chain's own result equals String.getBytes(name). The gold's javadoc promises the characters of the key encoded with the given charset, which FE FF 00 41 00 42 is not for "ABC" in UTF-16. A one-line hop edit that rewrites UTF-16 as UTF-16BE with an explicit U+FEFF first char passes the existing tests only because that estimate happens to be exact; it leaves every other text whose encoding exceeds its estimate cut short (getBytesUnchecked("\u00e9", "UTF-8") gives an empty array) and no longer encodes with the given charset as the hop's javadoc says.
